```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
library(bayesnec)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)
```

## Background

The posterior draws a Bayesian fit produces are useful well beyond a point
estimate. They support the study of synergistic and antagonistic effects
[@Fisher2019d; @flores2021], the propagation of endpoint uncertainty
[@Charles2020a; @Gottschalk2013], and tests of hypotheses of no effect
[@Thomas2006].

`compare_posterior()` uses them to compare fits: differences in a threshold
estimate such as the *NEC*, *NSEC* or an **EC~x~**, or differences across a
range of predictor values.

```{r}
#| label: fig-context
#| out-width: "48%"
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(c("images/dredging_effects.JPG", "images/herbicides_climate.JPG"))
```

## The data

Earlier modules used simulated data. This one works through a real analysis:
estimating no-effect concentrations for a set of herbicides and comparing their
relative toxicity.

The data are from @jones2003meps and ship with `bayesnec`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-source
#| out-width: "48%"
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(c("images/jonesnkerswell.jpg", "images/s_hystrix.jpg"))
```

The response is the maximum effective quantum yield, $\Delta F / Fm'$, of
symbiotic dinoflagellates in the tissue of the coral *Seriatopora hystrix*,
calculated from chlorophyll fluorescence measured with a DIVING-PAM fluorometer
[@jones2003meps; @jones2003effects]. Corals were exposed for 10 hours to eight
herbicides at concentrations from 0.3 to 1000 $\mu g L^{-1}$. Ioxynil is
excluded here because it produced no adequate response at the highest
concentration, leaving seven.

```{r}
#| label: data
data(herbicide)
str(herbicide)
table(herbicide$herbicide)
```

## How these fits were produced

Seven herbicides fitted against the `decline` set is
`r length(models()$decline)` equations each, and takes hours. These fits are
therefore **not run when this page is built**. They are produced by
`scripts/generate_herbicide_fits.R`, which writes the compact results this
module reads. The fitted objects themselves are far too large to keep — the
2023 equivalent was 451 MB.

The code shown below is the code that was run. It is displayed rather than
executed, and every result on this page comes from that run.

```{r}
#| label: provenance
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
cat(readLines("data/herbicide_provenance.txt"), sep = "\n")
```

## Fitting one herbicide

Taking ametryn first. The concentration is log transformed before fitting, both
because it stabilises the fit and because the concentration series is
logarithmic by design. There is little evidence of hormesis in these data, so
the `decline` set is used rather than the full set.

```{r}
#| label: fit-ametryn-shown
#| eval: false
ametryn <- herbicide |>
  mutate(concentration = log(concentration)) |>
  filter(herbicide == "ametryn")

manecfit_ametryn <- bnec(fvfm ~ crf(concentration, model = "decline"),
                         data = ametryn, seed = 17)
```

Every argument other than the model set is left at its default. `bayesnec`
selects a beta distribution for the response, uses the identity link, and drops
`neclin` and `ecxlin` from the `decline` set because they are not suitable for a
zero-bounded distribution.

### The summary

```{r}
#| label: ametryn-summary
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
cat(readLines("data/ametryn_summary.txt"), sep = "\n")
```

The weights are spread across several smooth equations with limited support for
the threshold models. The no-effect estimate is reported on the log
concentration scale, because that is the scale the model was fitted on.

### Every equation in the set

```{r}
#| label: fig-ametryn-all
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Each equation fitted to the ametryn data, with its 95% credible interval."
allmods <- read.csv("data/ametryn_allmodels.csv")

ggplot(allmods, aes(x = concentration)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Q2.5, ymax = Q97.5), fill = "grey80") +
  geom_line(aes(y = Estimate)) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log",
                     breaks = c(0.3, 3, 30, 300)) +
  labs(x = expression("Concentration ("*mu*"g/L)"),
       y = expression(Delta*"F/Fm'")) +
  theme_classic()
```

Fits should also be checked with `check_chains()` and `check_priors()`, as
modules 4 and 6 describe. Both take a `filename`, which writes the plots to a
PDF suitable for an analysis appendix rather than to the screen.

## Fitting all seven

The same call is applied to each herbicide in turn.

```{r}
#| label: fit-all-shown
#| eval: false
manecfit <- herbicide |>
  mutate(concentration = log(concentration)) |>
  split(f = ~ herbicide) |>
  purrr::map(function(x) {
    bnec(fvfm ~ crf(concentration, model = "decline"), data = x, seed = 17)
  })
```

### Dropping models that did not converge

Any model failing the R-hat criterion is removed with `amend()`.

```{r}
#| label: clean-shown
#| eval: false
failed_models <- function(fit) {
  r <- rhat(fit)
  names(which(vapply(r, function(z) isTRUE(z$failed), logical(1))))
}

cleaned_fits <- purrr::map(manecfit, function(fit) {
  bad <- failed_models(fit)
  if (length(bad) > 0) amend(fit, drop = bad) else fit
})
```

`rhat()` on a `bayesmanecfit` returns a list keyed by model name, each element
holding the R-hat values and a logical `failed`. It is worth extracting it as
above rather than reaching for `rhat(fit)$failed`, which is `NULL` on that
structure and silently drops nothing. The default cutoff is 1.01.

```{r}
#| label: failed-models
#| echo: false
failed <- read.csv("data/herbicide_rhat_failed.csv")
if (nrow(failed) == 0) {
  cat("No model failed the R-hat criterion.\n")
} else {
  kable(failed, caption = "Models dropped for failing the R-hat criterion.")
}
```

## Model weights across herbicides

```{r}
#| label: tbl-weights
#| tbl-cap: "Fitted models and their relative weights, for the effect of seven herbicides on the maximum effective quantum yield of symbiotic dinoflagellates of *Seriatopora hystrix*."
modstats <- read.csv("data/herbicide_mod_stats.csv")

modstats |>
  mutate(wi = round(wi, 3)) |>
  select(herbicide, model, wi) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = herbicide, values_from = wi) |>
  kable()
```

The best-fitting equations differ substantially between herbicides. Few show
much weight on the threshold models. Among the smooth equations the weights vary
widely, with support for more than one in every case.

That is the argument for model averaging in a sentence: there is no single
equation that is right for these data, the best one differs by herbicide, and
selecting one would discard the uncertainty about which. Averaging carries it
through into the estimates instead.

Some models failed to fit under the default settings for every herbicide. Custom
priors or initial values would likely recover them, but with a large number of
well-fitting models already in each set, doing so is unlikely to change the
inference.

## The fitted curves

```{r}
#| label: fig-all-herbicides
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Model-averaged concentration-response curves for seven herbicides, with 95% credible intervals and the observations."
preds <- read.csv("data/herbicide_pred_vals.csv")
obs   <- read.csv("data/herbicide_observations.csv")

ggplot(preds, aes(x = concentration)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Q2.5, ymax = Q97.5), fill = "grey80") +
  geom_line(aes(y = Estimate)) +
  geom_point(data = obs, aes(y = fvfm), size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ herbicide, ncol = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log", breaks = c(0.3, 3, 30, 300)) +
  labs(x = expression("Concentration ("*mu*"g/L)"),
       y = expression(Delta*"F/Fm'")) +
  theme_classic()
```

## The toxicity estimates

The value reported for each herbicide is a model-averaged posterior combining
the *NEC* parameter from the threshold equations with the *NSEC* from the smooth
ones, which is what module 3 described. It is labelled N(S)EC for that reason.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-estimates
#| tbl-cap: "Model-averaged no-effect estimates, back-transformed to concentration."
read.csv("data/herbicide_estimates.csv") |>
  transmute(Herbicide = herbicide,
            `Estimate` = signif(estimate, 3),
            `Lower 95%` = signif(lower, 3),
            `Upper 95%` = signif(upper, 3)) |>
  kable()
```

These are the estimates that would enter a guideline derivation. In Australia
that is the Australian and New Zealand Water Quality Guidelines [@anzg], where
the *NEC* is the established preference [@Warne2015; @warne2018] and use of the
*NSEC* is recent [@Fisher2022] and not yet formally adopted.

```{r}
#| label: fig-nsecieam
#| out-width: "34%"
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("images/NSEC_ieam.jpg")
```

## Comparing the posteriors

`compare_posterior()` extracts the weighted posterior for each fit so they can
be compared directly, rather than by asking whether intervals overlap.

```{r}
#| label: compare-shown
#| eval: false
post_comp <- compare_posterior(cleaned_fits, comparison = "nec")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-posteriors
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Posterior densities of the N(S)EC estimate for each herbicide."
post <- read.csv("data/herbicide_ne_posterior.csv")

ggplot(post, aes(x = concentration, group = model,
                 colour = model, fill = model)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.3) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log", breaks = c(0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30),
                     labels = c(0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30)) +
  labs(x = expression("Concentration ("*mu*"g/L)"), y = "Density",
       colour = "Herbicide", fill = "Herbicide") +
  theme_classic()
```

Irgarol, diuron and ametryn are the most toxic and are similar to one another,
their densities overlapping substantially. Tebuthiuron is the least toxic,
followed by simazine and atrazine, with hexazinone intermediate.

## Probabilities of difference

Overlapping densities are a visual impression. `compare_posterior()` also
returns the probability that one estimate is lower than another, computed from
the draws.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-probdiff
#| tbl-cap: "Probability of difference in no-effect toxicity between herbicides, from the overlap in their posterior densities."
read.csv("data/herbicide_prob_diff.csv") |>
  separate(col = comparison, into = c("herbicide", "against"), sep = "-") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = against, values_from = prob) |>
  kable()
```

This is the practical advantage of having the posterior rather than an interval.
The question "is A more toxic than B" is answered with a probability computed
from the draws, without a significance test, and it propagates the uncertainty
in the curve shape as well as in the parameters.
